items.stimulus:
An old puzzle, usually traced to the Greek writer Plutarch, asks us to imagine a famous wooden ship kept in a harbour as a memorial. As each plank rots, it is removed and replaced with a new one, until eventually not a single original plank remains. Is the restored vessel still the same ship? Many people answer yes, pointing out that the ship never stopped existing and kept the same shape, name and purpose throughout. Others insist that an object is nothing more than the material it is made of, so that once every part has been changed, the original has ceased to exist.

The seventeenth-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes sharpened the problem. Suppose, he asked, that someone collected the discarded planks and reassembled them in their original order. There would now be two ships, each with a strong claim to be the original: one has unbroken continuity of form, the other has all the original matter. Both cannot be the one ship, yet it is hard to say which claim should win.

The puzzle matters less for boats than for people. Many cells of the human body are continually replaced, though not all at the same rate, and some, including most neurons in the brain, can last a lifetime. Philosophers therefore rarely rest personal identity on physical matter alone. John Locke proposed instead that a person remains the same person as far back as their consciousness, and especially their memory, reaches. Later critics noted a difficulty. An elderly general might remember his deeds as a young officer, and the young officer might remember a childhood punishment, while the general has forgotten that childhood entirely. On Locke's view, the general would be the same person as the officer, and the officer the same as the child, yet the general would not be the same person as the child. This seems absurd, because if A is identical to B and B to C, then A should be identical to C.

Some modern thinkers conclude that the question 'Is it the same?' may have no single correct answer, and that what matters in survival is not strict identity but degrees of psychological connection.

items.stimulus:
Shoppers like to believe that they judge each product on its own merits, but a well-documented finding in behavioural economics suggests otherwise. When people choose between two options that differ in price and quality, their preferences can be shifted by adding a third option that almost nobody buys. This third option is known as a decoy, and the pattern it creates is called the decoy effect or asymmetric dominance.

Imagine an online photo-storage service that offers two monthly plans: 50 gigabytes for $3 and 200 gigabytes for $6. Many customers, seeing that the larger plan costs twice as much, settle for the smaller one. Now suppose the service adds a third plan offering 150 gigabytes for $6. This plan costs exactly the same as the 200-gigabyte plan but stores less, so it is plainly worse than that plan, while it is not clearly worse than the cheap plan. Its presence makes the 200-gigabyte plan look like a bargain, and sign-ups for that plan tend to rise even though the 150-gigabyte plan itself is rarely chosen.

The decoy works because people find absolute values hard to judge. It is difficult to know whether 200 gigabytes is really worth $6 a month, but easy to see that it beats 150 gigabytes at the same price. Faced with uncertainty, shoppers seize on the comparison that is easiest to make and treat it as a reason to choose.

Researchers have reported the effect in choices ranging from subscriptions to job candidates, yet it is not universal. Some studies suggest it is weaker when people already know the product well, when the decoy is too obviously inferior to be taken seriously, and when options are presented as pictures rather than as numbers. Several later studies have also failed to reproduce the largest effects reported in early experiments.

For consumers, the lesson is not that every three-tier price list is a trick; middle options often exist simply because some customers want them. The lesson is rather to ask, before buying, whether the option chosen would still seem attractive if the others vanished.

items.stimulus:
In Japan during the Edo period, colour woodblock prints known as ukiyo-e, or 'pictures of the floating world', were a commercial product rather than a prestigious art form. A single design passed through several hands: a publisher commissioned it, an artist drew it, a carver cut it into blocks of cherry wood, and a printer applied the colours, using a separate block for each colour. Because the blocks could be reused many times, prints of actors, beautiful women and landscapes were sold cheaply and in large numbers.

After Japan expanded its trade with Western nations in the 1850s, these prints reached Europe in growing quantities, and by the 1870s collecting them had become fashionable in Paris, where critics coined the word 'Japonisme' for the craze. A frequently repeated story holds that the first prints to excite French artists arrived as wrapping around imported porcelain. Historians regard the tale as possibly exaggerated, but it captures how modestly the prints were valued at home compared with the enthusiasm they met abroad.

What struck European painters was less the subject matter than the way the pictures were built. Ukiyo-e designers used flat areas of unshaded colour, strong outlines, and viewpoints from high above or unusually close. They often cut figures off abruptly at the edge of the frame and placed the main subject off centre. Such choices broke with the academic tradition in Europe, which valued modelling in light and shade and carefully balanced compositions.

Edgar Degas borrowed the abrupt cropping for his scenes of dancers and racecourses. Vincent van Gogh collected several hundred prints and made painted copies of works by Hiroshige, translating them into thick, vivid oil paint. Claude Monet hung Japanese prints throughout his house at Giverny. For these artists, the prints offered not an exotic theme to imitate but a demonstration that a picture could be organised in an entirely different way.

A satellite navigation receiver, such as the one in a mobile phone, does not send anything to the satellites overhead; it simply listens. Each satellite in a system such as the American GPS constellation carries highly accurate atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts a signal stating its own position and the exact time at which the signal left it. The receiver notes when each signal arrives, and because radio waves travel at the speed of light, the delay reveals how far away the satellite is. Light covers about 30 centimetres in a billionth of a second, so even tiny timing errors translate into large errors in distance.

Knowing its distance from one satellite places the receiver somewhere on an imaginary sphere centred on that satellite. Distances from three satellites narrow the possibilities to a single point near the Earth's surface. In practice, however, a fourth satellite is needed, because the inexpensive quartz clock in a phone is far less precise than the satellites' clocks. Treating its own clock error as an extra unknown, the receiver uses the fourth measurement to solve for that error alongside the three coordinates of its position.

The satellites' clocks raise a subtler problem, which can only be understood through Einstein's theories of relativity. Special relativity predicts that a clock moving fast relative to an observer will tick more slowly, and GPS satellites travel at roughly 14,000 kilometres per hour; on this account alone their clocks would lose about 7 microseconds a day. The net result is a gain of roughly 38 microseconds daily. Left uncorrected, this would allow position errors to build up by around 10 kilometres each day. In 1964 a young woman was murdered outside her apartment building in New York. A newspaper report claimed that 38 neighbours had watched or listened and done nothing, and the story became a symbol of urban indifference. Later investigations found that this account was badly exaggerated: few people saw the attack clearly, and at least one neighbour did call the police.

The case nonetheless prompted the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané to ask whether the mere presence of others makes people less likely to help. items.stimulus:
Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are eight-legged animals usually less than a millimetre long. Although some live in the sea, many inhabit the thin films of water that cling to moss and lichen, habitats that can dry out completely within hours. Their survival in such places depends on a state called anhydrobiosis, a form of cryptobiosis in which life is suspended rather than ended.

As its surroundings dry, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and contracts into a compact, barrel-shaped form known as a tun. It loses almost all of its body water, and its metabolism falls so low that it cannot be detected. In this condition it can endure extreme cold, high temperatures and doses of radiation that would kill most animals. When water returns, many individuals become active again within hours, apparently none the worse.

How the animal avoids being damaged by drying has been studied intensively. Some other animals that survive desiccation, such as certain brine shrimp, rely heavily on a sugar called trehalose, which turns into a glass-like solid that holds the contents of cells in place. One species also makes a protein that binds to its DNA and reduces damage from radiation.

The tun is not a magic shield. The process works only if drying is gradual; a tardigrade dried too quickly may never revive. Merchants travelled in caravans, groups that could include dozens or even hundreds of animals, for protection against bandits and the hazards of the road. Inside, an open courtyard was surrounded by rooms for travellers and storage, with stabling for animals on the ground floor or in covered halls. Many had a well or cistern, and some included a small mosque and a bath. The thick walls and single entrance made the building easy to defend, and the gate could be closed at night.

Caravanserais were usually spaced about a day's journey apart, often thirty to forty kilometres, so that a caravan could move from one to the next between sunrise and sunset. In thirteenth-century Anatolia, the Seljuk sultans built a chain of them along major routes, and some offered free food and lodging for a few days, an investment that encouraged trade and the taxes it produced. These buildings were more than shelters. items.stimulus:
For centuries, goods moved across the dry interior of Asia, the Middle East and North Africa on the backs of camels, horses and mules. Merchants travelled in caravans, groups that could include dozens or even hundreds of animals, for protection against bandits and the hazards of the road. To support this traffic, rulers and wealthy patrons built caravanserais: walled roadside inns where travellers, animals and cargo could rest overnight.

The typical caravanserai was a square or rectangular building with a single large gateway, high enough to admit a loaded camel. Inside, an open courtyard was surrounded by rooms for travellers and storage, with stabling for animals on the ground floor or in covered halls. Many had a well or cistern, and some included a small mosque and a bath. The thick walls and single entrance made the building easy to defend, and the gate could be closed at night.

Caravanserais were usually spaced about a day's journey apart, often thirty to forty kilometres, so that a caravan could move from one to the next between sunrise and sunset. In thirteenth-century Anatolia, the Seljuk sultans built a chain of them along major routes, and some offered free food and lodging for a few days, an investment that encouraged trade and the taxes it produced. In Persia, the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I ordered the construction of many more around 1600.

These buildings were more than shelters. Merchants who might never otherwise have met exchanged goods, prices and news in their courtyards, and travellers carried languages, religious ideas, techniques and sometimes diseases from one region to another. A caravanserai was, in effect, a node in a network that stretched across continents.

The decline of overland caravan trade came gradually, as sea routes carried more long-distance cargo and, much later, railways and roads replaced pack animals. Many caravanserais fell into ruin, though some have been restored as museums, markets or hotels.

items.stimulus:
Reef-building corals are animals, but most of them depend on a kind of plant partner. Inside the cells of their tissue live microscopic algae that photosynthesise and pass much of the sugar they make to their host, supplying most of the coral's energy needs in exchange for shelter and nutrients. The algae also give many corals their colour.

This partnership is sensitive to heat. When sea temperatures rise only about one degree Celsius above the usual summer maximum and stay there for several weeks, the relationship breaks down. The stressed algae begin producing harmful compounds, and the coral expels them from its tissue. Without the algae, the tissue becomes nearly transparent and the white limestone skeleton shows through. This is coral bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead. If temperatures fall soon enough, it can take up algae again from the surrounding water and recover over the following months. But it is starving in the meantime, and if heat stress is severe or prolonged, many corals die. Even those that survive often grow and reproduce less for a time and are more vulnerable to disease.

Scientists track heat stress with a measure called degree heating weeks, which combines how far temperatures exceed the normal summer maximum with how long they stay there. Higher values are associated with more widespread bleaching and death. Marine heatwaves, periods of unusually warm water lasting from days to months, have become more frequent as the oceans have warmed, and mass bleaching events affecting reefs across hundreds of kilometres have occurred repeatedly in recent decades.

The interval between events is critical. Fast-growing corals can recolonise a damaged reef within about a decade, while slow-growing massive corals take much longer. If severe bleaching returns every few years, reefs may never fully recover, and their mix of species may shift towards those that cope best with disturbance.

items.stimulus:
In the 1840s the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics. The first was staffed by doctors and medical students, the second by midwives, and women were admitted to them on alternate days. Ignaz Semmelweis, a young Hungarian physician working in the first clinic, was troubled by a stark difference: deaths from childbed fever, a severe infection after delivery, were several times higher in his clinic than in the midwives' clinic. Women knew this, and some begged not to be admitted to the first.

Semmelweis tested and rejected one explanation after another. The breakthrough came in 1847, when a colleague died of an illness resembling childbed fever after cutting his finger during a post-mortem examination. Semmelweis reasoned that doctors and students, who often came straight from dissecting bodies to examining women in labour, were carrying some harmful material on their hands. Midwives did not perform post-mortems. He required staff to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and the death rate in the first clinic fell dramatically, to roughly the level of the second.

Yet his idea won little acceptance during his lifetime. It challenged prevailing theories of disease, and it implied that physicians themselves had been causing deaths. Semmelweis also published a full account only years later and often answered critics with angry letters rather than persuasive evidence. Only after the work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister established that microorganisms cause infection was he widely recognised as a pioneer. His story is often told as that of a lone genius ignored, but it is also a reminder that a correct finding needs clear communication if it is to change practice.

items.stimulus:
In many common-law countries, including Australia, serious criminal charges have traditionally been decided by a jury: a group of ordinary citizens, usually twelve, chosen at random from the community. In some places, however, an accused person may in certain circumstances ask to be tried by a judge sitting alone. The option raises a long-standing debate about who is best placed to decide guilt.

Supporters of juries argue that they bring community values into the courtroom and act as a check on state power, since a conviction requires the agreement of people with no professional stake in the system. Twelve people also bring a range of life experience to the task of judging whether a witness is believable.

Critics reply that jurors have no legal training, may struggle with long or technical evidence such as complex financial records, and can be swayed by publicity about a case before the trial begins. A judge, by contrast, is experienced in weighing evidence and is expected to set aside prejudicial material.

A practical difference concerns reasons. A jury announces its verdict without explaining how it was reached, and its discussions are kept secret. A judge sitting alone must give reasons, which can then be examined on appeal. Some see this as a decisive advantage of judge-only trials; others point out that the judge is still one person, whose particular outlook is not balanced by eleven others.

Accused people choose judge-only trials for varied reasons, for example when a case has attracted intense media coverage or when the defence rests on a technical legal argument. Whether such trials lead to more or fewer convictions overall is difficult to judge, because the cases in which they are chosen differ from those that go to juries.

items.stimulus: A farmers' cooperative supplies meal boxes to the pilots of a small charter airline, which is a member of the cooperative. The pricing rules are: each meal box costs $12.00; an order of 10 or more boxes receives 10% off the whole order; members then receive a further $1.00 off each box, applied after any percentage discount; delivery costs $15.00 unless the order total after all discounts is more than $150.00, in which case delivery is free.
items.question: The airline orders 12 meal boxes to be delivered. What is the total amount it pays?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 기본 금액: 12 × 12 = $144.00. 10상자 이상이므로 10% 할인: 144 × 0.9 = $129.60. 2) 회원 할인은 퍼센트 할인 뒤에 상자당 $1: 129.60 − 12 = $117.60. 3) 할인 후 금액이 $150 이하이므로 배송비 $15를 더한다: 117.60 + 15 = $132.60. 오답: A는 배송비를 빠뜨린 값, B는 회원 할인과 배송비를 모두 빠뜨린 값, D는 $1 할인을 퍼센트 할인보다 먼저 적용한 값((12 − 1) × 12 × 0.9 + 15)으로 적용 순서를 어긴 것이다. → 정답 C
